column2: Which statement correctly defines a Type I error?
column3: A Type I error occurs when the null hypothesis is false and the test fails to reject it.
column4: A Type I error occurs when the null hypothesis is true and the test rejects it.
column5: A Type I error occurs when the alternative hypothesis is true and the test rejects the null correctly.
column6: A Type I error occurs when the p-value is greater than alpha and the sample size is small.

column2: Which statement correctly defines a Type II error?
column3: A Type II error occurs when the null hypothesis is true and the test rejects it.
column4: A Type II error occurs when the null hypothesis is true and the test correctly fails to reject it.
column5: A Type II error occurs when the alternative hypothesis is false and the test rejects the null.
column6: A Type II error occurs when the null hypothesis is false and the test fails to reject it.

column2: In significance testing, what is a false positive?
column3: A false positive is a Type I error because the test claims evidence for the alternative when the null is actually true.
column4: A false positive is a Type II error because the test misses a real effect.
column5: A false positive is a correct decision because the test rejected a false null hypothesis.
column6: A false positive is the same thing as choosing a large significance level.

column2: In significance testing, what is a false negative?
column3: A false negative is a Type I error because the test rejects a true null hypothesis.
column4: A false negative is a correct decision because the test fails to reject a true null hypothesis.
column5: A false negative is a Type II error because the test misses a real alternative hypothesis.
column6: A false negative is the same thing as using a p-value equal to alpha.

column2: If the p-value is less than or equal to alpha, what is the correct conclusion?
column3: The correct conclusion is to fail to reject the null hypothesis because the result could happen by chance.
column4: The correct conclusion is to accept the null hypothesis because the p-value is small.
column5: The correct conclusion is to say both the null and alternative hypotheses are supported equally.
column6: The correct conclusion is to reject the null hypothesis and say there is convincing statistical evidence for the alternative hypothesis.

column2: If the p-value is greater than alpha, what is the correct conclusion?
column3: The correct conclusion is to fail to reject the null hypothesis because there is not convincing statistical evidence for the alternative hypothesis.
column4: The correct conclusion is to reject the null hypothesis because a large p-value shows the alternative is likely.
column5: The correct conclusion is to accept the null hypothesis because the data proved it to be true.
column6: The correct conclusion is to reject the alternative hypothesis because the sample was not extreme enough.

column2: Which outcome occurs when the null hypothesis is true and the test fails to reject it?
column3: This outcome is a Type I error because the test should have rejected the null hypothesis.
column4: This outcome is a correct decision because the test did not reject a null hypothesis that was actually true.
column5: This outcome is a Type II error because the alternative hypothesis must be true.
column6: This outcome is power because the test avoided a false positive.

column2: Which outcome occurs when the alternative hypothesis is true and the test rejects the null hypothesis?
column3: This outcome is a Type I error because the test rejected the null hypothesis.
column4: This outcome is a Type II error because the test made a decision under uncertainty.
column5: This outcome is a correct decision because the test rejected a false null hypothesis.
column6: This outcome is impossible because the true state of nature can never match the decision.

column2: How should a Type I error be interpreted in context?
column3: A Type I error means we found convincing evidence for the alternative claim in context even though that claim is not actually true.
column4: A Type I error means we proved the null hypothesis is true in the context of the study.
column5: A Type I error means we found the sample statistic exactly equal to the null value in context.
column6: A Type I error means we should describe the result only with symbols and not with the study wording.

column2: Which hypotheses match the green-cup lemonade study?
column3: The hypotheses are H0: p > 0.50 and Ha: p = 0.50, where p is the proportion of all students who would choose the green cup.
column4: The hypotheses are H0: p = 0.64 and Ha: p = 0.45, where p is the power of the test.
column5: The hypotheses are H0: p = 0.50 and Ha: p is not equal to 0.50, where p is the proportion of all students who would choose the white cup.
column6: The hypotheses are H0: p = 0.50 and Ha: p > 0.50, where p is the proportion of all students who would choose the green cup.

column2: Which statement describes a Type I error in the green-cup study?
column3: The researchers do not find convincing evidence that more than 50% of students would choose the green cup even though the true percentage is above 50%.
column4: The researchers conclude that more than 50% of students would choose the green cup even though the true percentage is actually 50%.
column5: The researchers conclude that exactly 50% of students choose the green cup because both cups contained the same lemonade.
column6: The researchers conclude that fewer than 50% of students would choose the green cup because the sample happened to favor white.

column2: Which statement describes a Type II error in the green-cup study?
column3: The researchers conclude that more than 50% of students would choose the green cup even though the true percentage is 50%.
column4: The researchers correctly fail to reject the null hypothesis when exactly 50% of students would choose the green cup.
column5: The researchers do not find convincing evidence that more than 50% of students would choose the green cup even though the true percentage is above 50%.
column6: The researchers reject the null hypothesis because the green cup looks more natural to some students.

column2: In the marketing example from the lesson, which error was more consequential and why?
column3: A Type I error was more consequential because the company might spend money using green even when green does not actually change what people think.
column4: A Type II error was more consequential because the company might miss a useful branding strategy and lose potential sales.
column5: Neither error was consequential because both cups contained the same brand of lemonade.
column6: A Type I error was more consequential because false positives are always worse than false negatives.

column2: When the null hypothesis is true, what is the probability of a Type I error?
column3: The probability of a Type I error is equal to the significance level alpha.
column4: The probability of a Type I error is equal to 1 minus the power.
column5: The probability of a Type I error is equal to the sample size divided by the standard error.
column6: The probability of a Type I error is equal to the p-value from the sample.

column2: Why should the consequences of a Type I error influence the choice of alpha?
column3: The consequences of a Type I error should influence alpha because alpha controls the sample size directly.
column4: The consequences of a Type I error should influence alpha because alpha is the probability of a Type II error.
column5: The consequences of a Type I error should influence alpha because alpha and power are always equal.
column6: The consequences of a Type I error should influence alpha because alpha is the probability of making that false-positive error.

column2: Why would setting alpha = 0.0000001 usually be a bad default choice?
column3: Setting alpha that small would guarantee perfect power and eliminate both types of errors.
column4: Setting alpha that small would change the meaning of the null hypothesis.
column5: Setting alpha that small would make rejecting the null hypothesis extremely hard and would increase the chance of a Type II error.
column6: Setting alpha that small would matter only when the null hypothesis is false, so it would not affect most tests.

column2: All other things being equal, what happens when we decrease the probability of a Type I error?
column3: All other things being equal, decreasing the probability of a Type I error increases the probability of a Type II error.
column4: All other things being equal, decreasing the probability of a Type I error also decreases the probability of a Type II error.
column5: All other things being equal, decreasing the probability of a Type I error leaves the probability of a Type II error unchanged.
column6: All other things being equal, decreasing the probability of a Type I error makes the two error probabilities add up to 0.50.

column2: What is the power of a test?
column3: The power of a test is the probability that the null hypothesis is true after seeing the data.
column4: The power of a test is the probability of making a Type I error.
column5: The power of a test is the probability that the p-value equals the significance level.
column6: The power of a test is the probability that the test correctly rejects a false null hypothesis.

column2: Which statement about power is correct?
column3: Power is the probability that the test fails to reject the null hypothesis when the null is true.
column4: Power is the probability of finding convincing evidence for the alternative hypothesis when the alternative is actually true.
column5: Power is the same quantity as alpha in every significance test.
column6: Power is the probability that the sample statistic matches the population parameter exactly.

column2: How is the probability of a Type II error related to power?
column3: The probability of a Type II error is equal to alpha because both are error probabilities.
column4: The probability of a Type II error is equal to power because both describe missing the alternative.
column5: The probability of a Type II error is equal to 1 minus power because power measures avoiding that error.
column6: The probability of a Type II error is equal to 1 minus alpha because the two errors are complements.

column2: If the power against p = 0.64 is 0.45 in the green-cup study, what does that mean?
column3: It means there is a 0.45 probability that the null hypothesis is true when p = 0.64.
column4: It means there is a 0.45 probability that exactly 45% of students would choose the green cup.
column5: It means there is a 0.45 probability that the p-value will be 0.64.
column6: It means there is a 0.45 probability of finding convincing evidence that more than 50% of students would choose the green cup when the true proportion is 0.64.

column2: If alpha = 0.05 and the power is 0.45, what is the probability of a Type II error?
column3: The probability of a Type II error is 0.55 because it is equal to 1 minus the power.
column4: The probability of a Type II error is 0.45 because power and Type II error are the same number.
column5: The probability of a Type II error is 0.05 because it matches the significance level.
column6: The probability of a Type II error is 0.50 because alpha and power must average to one-half.

column2: Which change would increase the power of a test, all else being equal?
column3: Decreasing the sample size would increase power because smaller samples produce more extreme outcomes.
column4: Keeping the sample size the same would always keep the power at exactly 0.50.
column5: Increasing the sample size would increase power because more data make real effects easier to detect.
column6: Changing the sample size would affect only alpha and would not affect power.

column2: Which statement correctly describes how alpha affects power, all else being equal?
column3: Decreasing alpha increases power because stricter evidence leads to more rejections of the null hypothesis.
column4: Increasing alpha increases power because it becomes easier for the p-value to fall below the cutoff.
column5: Changing alpha does not affect power because power depends only on the sample size.
column6: Keeping alpha at 0.05 guarantees the maximum possible power in every setting.

column2: How does standard error affect power, all else being equal?
column3: Decreasing the standard error increases power because less variability makes a real difference easier to detect.
column4: Increasing the standard error increases power because more variability creates more signal.
column5: Standard error affects confidence intervals only, so it does not affect power.
column6: Standard error changes Type I error but cannot change Type II error.

column2: How does the distance between the true parameter value and the null value affect power?
column3: Power is greatest when the true parameter value is exactly equal to the null value.
column4: The distance from the null value does not matter because power depends only on alpha.
column5: Power decreases when the true parameter value moves farther from the null value because extreme results become less stable.
column6: Power increases when the true parameter value is farther from the null value because larger differences are easier to detect.

column2: Which of the following is NOT one of the four factors from the lesson that affect power?
column3: The sample size is one of the factors that affect power.
column4: The significance level is one of the factors that affect power.
column5: The color used to write the hypotheses is not one of the factors that affect power.
column6: The standard error is one of the factors that affect power.

column2: Which situation is a Type II error?
column3: Rejecting the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually true is a Type II error.
column4: Failing to reject the null hypothesis when the alternative hypothesis is actually true is a Type II error.
column5: Rejecting the null hypothesis when the alternative hypothesis is actually true is a Type II error.
column6: Failing to reject the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually true is a Type II error.

column2: Which of these is NOT a true statement about the power of a significance test?
column3: Power depends on the true parameter value when that value differs from the null.
column4: Power is larger when the sample size is larger, all else being equal.
column5: Power helps describe the chance of avoiding a Type II error.
column6: Power is the probability that the null hypothesis is false.

column2: Which statement about the consequences of Type I and Type II errors is correct?
column3: Which error is more consequential depends on the context and on the real-world costs of each mistake.
column4: A Type I error is always more consequential than a Type II error in every setting.
column5: A Type II error is always more consequential than a Type I error in every setting.
column6: The two errors always have identical consequences because both are statistical mistakes.
